name: Bias in Clinical Triage
title: Bias in Clinical Triage
answer: Bias in clinical triage covers systematic differences in how automated systems rank urgency, assign acuity scores, or allocate scarce resources such as beds, imaging, or specialist review. It includes emergency department intake, telehealth symptom checkers, pre-hospital dispatch, and mass casualty or pandemic triage. The concern is not only statistical error but differential harm: a model may under-triage some groups for heart attack or sepsis while over-triaging others. The site's registry of 1000 medical AI models provides a broad view of where triage tools are deployed and where bias audits are needed.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems typically run on electronic health record data, patient-entered symptoms, vital signs, laboratory results, and sometimes wearable or remote monitoring feeds. They are served through hospital EHR modules, FHIR-based APIs, call center software, or standalone triage applications, often with a human clinician in the loop. Bias can enter through missing values, inconsistent measurement, legacy billing codes that stand in for clinical facts, or interfaces that collect less detail from certain patient groups. The same model may perform differently across sites because of differences in population mix, equipment, or documentation practice.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Bias work in triage usually begins with subgroup analysis: comparing false negative and false positive rates, calibration, and acuity assignment across age, sex, race, language, payer, and comorbidity groups. Teams also use counterfactual testing, where a patient's protected attribute is changed while clinical facts stay the same, to see whether the triage score shifts. Common technical responses include reweighting training data, adjusting decision thresholds by subgroup, or adding fairness constraints during model training. Because triage outcomes are time-sensitive, evaluation often focuses on near-miss events, delayed escalation, and resource denial rather than only overall accuracy.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Clinical triage models may be regulated as medical devices, and in many jurisdictions they must meet requirements for validation, labeling, and postmarket monitoring. Bias is also a compliance issue under health privacy and nondiscrimination rules, and hospitals may need to document how a triage tool was selected, audited, and overridden. The site tracks six active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, which shows how biased or poorly validated triage can become a legal risk. Provenance records, including training data sources, exclusion criteria, and model version history, are part of audit trails for clinical safety teams. Patients generally have rights to know when automated triage is used and to have a human review the decision.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward continuous bias monitoring rather than one-time premarket checks, with live dashboards that compare triage decisions and outcomes across subgroups. Federated learning and multi-site registries may allow bias audits without pooling sensitive patient data. Regulators and standards bodies are working on triage-specific fairness benchmarks, including acceptable differences in under-triage rates for high-risk conditions. Explainable triage scores and routine human override review are likely to become standard, along with postmarket surveillance that flags drift when a model encounters new populations or care pathways.
